1100.title: The fruits of Communion (CCC 1391–1401)
1100.hook: union with Christ, forgiveness of venial sin, unity, care for the poor
1100.howItsDone: After receiving Communion, Catholics spend a few moments in silent thanksgiving; some parishes take up a collection for the poor at Mass or keep food bins by the church doors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the real presence: Christ present in many ways, and above all under the bread and wine. Your line was truly, really, substantially.

Right after Communion, the Mass goes quiet. People file back from the front and kneel or sit. Some close their eyes. A child swings her feet. The organist plays something soft, or nothing at all. It can look like nothing is happening. The Catechism disagrees. It lists what Communion does in a person, and the list doesn't stop at the pew. It ends somewhere unexpected: out on the street, with people who are hungry.
screen: `THE QUIET AFTER COMMUNION.` → `IT LOOKS LIKE NOTHING.` → `THE LIST ENDS ON THE STREET.`

segments.voice: First, union with Christ. The Catechism quotes Jesus in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, abideth in me, and I in him." Abiding: staying, living with. What bread does for the body, Communion does for the life of grace begun at baptism: it keeps it, grows it, renews it. Second, separation from sin. The body given up for us and the blood shed for the forgiveness of sins can't unite people to Christ without also cleansing them. Communion strengthens charity, the Catechism says, and charity wipes away venial sins, the everyday ones, and helps protect against grave sin in the future. It's careful to add that Communion isn't meant for forgiving mortal sins; that belongs to the sacrament of penance. Third, unity. Paul puts it in one line: "For we, being many, are one bread, one body, all that partake of one bread." So the Eucharist makes the Church. Receiving Christ's body joins people to everyone else who receives it. And last, the one on the street. To receive in truth the body and blood of Christ given up for us, the Catechism says, we must recognize Christ in the poorest, his brothers and sisters. It cites John Chrysostom, who warned people who had tasted the Lord's blood against failing to recognize their own brother in need. Then, honestly, the section ends with a sorrow: Christians who can't yet share one table, and a hope that they one day will.
screen: `UNION: ABIDETH IN ME.` · `SEPARATION FROM SIN.` · `UNITY: ONE BREAD, ONE BODY.` · `THE POOR: CHRIST'S BROTHERS AND SISTERS.` · then, large: `WE, BEING MANY, ARE ONE BREAD.`

segments.voice: Think of the walk out of church, or out of your front door: someone asking for change, a food bank bin, a neighbor who's struggling and doesn't say so. Choose one concrete gift, money, food, an hour, a phone call, small enough that you'll really give it, and hold that person or place in mind while you breathe. If you pray, bring them to the altar with you.
The fruits of Communion. Union with Christ, separation from sin, unity in one body, and care for the poor, his brothers and sisters. Today's word.
Your line: communion makes communion. The table and the street belong together. Until tomorrow.

1101.title: Conversion (CCC 1427–1433)
1101.hook: conversion is a lifelong turning of the heart
1101.howItsDone: Catholics speak of daily conversion and mark it in the examination of conscience, the penitential act at the start of Mass, Lent, and the sacrament of reconciliation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fruits of Communion: union, separation from sin, one body, and the poor. Your line was communion makes communion.

A courtyard at night, a fire, a servant girl staring. Peter has said it three times now: he doesn't know the man. Somewhere a cock crows. Then comes a line in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, so short it's easy to read past: "And the Lord turning looked on Peter." Peter remembers what Jesus told him, goes outside, and weeps bitterly. This wasn't his first day as a disciple; he'd left his boats long before. And still, here, he turns again.
screen: `A COURTYARD, A FIRE.` → `THREE DENIALS.` → `THE LORD TURNING LOOKED ON PETER.`

segments.voice: Day sixty-two told this night as a story; today, the Catechism's word for it: conversion. Mark's Gospel opens Jesus's preaching with it, in the Douay-Rheims: "The time is accomplished, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent, and believe the gospel." That call comes first to people who don't yet know Christ, the Catechism says, and the first, deep conversion happens in baptism. But it doesn't end there. It speaks of a second conversion, an uninterrupted task for the whole Church, which, quoting the Second Vatican Council, it calls holy and always in need of purification. So conversion isn't a moment you get through once. It's a direction. And it isn't mainly a human effort. It's the movement of a contrite heart, drawn and moved by grace to answer God's merciful love. Peter is the picture: after three denials, a look of infinite mercy draws tears of repentance from him. Joel, in the Douay-Rheims: "rend your hearts, and not your garments." The call is first to an interior turning, not outward works like sackcloth and ashes, though without a change of heart those works would be empty, and with one they follow. It's a reorientation of the whole life: away from evil, toward God, with real sorrow and the hope of mercy. And the Catechism is honest that the human heart is heavy and hard, so God has to give a new one. It quotes Lamentations: "Convert us, O Lord, to thee, and we shall be converted." Even the turning is a gift.
screen: `REPENT, AND BELIEVE THE GOSPEL.` · `A SECOND CONVERSION, NEVER FINISHED.` · `REND YOUR HEARTS.` · `EVEN THE TURNING IS A GIFT.` · then, large: `CONVERT US, O LORD, TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Let one small thing come to mind that's been pointing the wrong way: a habit of sharpness with one person, a lie that makes life easier, a grudge you're feeding. Picture yourself turning to face the other way, the way you'd turn your whole body toward someone who called your name. If you pray, ask God for that turn, with the words of Lamentations or in silence; if you don't, just hold the image of turning.
Conversion. A turning of the whole heart toward God, begun in baptism, never finished, and itself a gift of grace. Today's word.
Your line: keep turning. Peter turned, and then kept turning, for the rest of the story. Same time tomorrow.

1102.title: Many forms of penance (CCC 1434–1439)
1102.hook: fasting, prayer, almsgiving, reconciliation, care for the poor
1102.howItsDone: Catholics keep penance through fasting and abstinence in Lent and on Fridays, through prayer and giving to the poor, and through everyday acts of reconciliation and charity, alongside the sacrament of confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, conversion: a turning of the heart that goes on for a lifetime. Your line was keep turning.

A rosary prayed on a long bus ride. A skipped lunch on a Friday. Coins dropped into a box by the church door. A phone call to a brother after a long silence. A quiet hour at a soup kitchen. Lined up like that, they look like five different hobbies. The Catechism puts acts like these on one list. The turning of the heart doesn't stay inside, it says. It comes out through the hands, the mouth, the wallet, the calendar, and in more than one shape.
screen: `A ROSARY, FASTING, COINS, A PHONE CALL.` → `ONE LIST.` → `THE TURNING COMES OUT.`

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred thirty-six, penance was the small task given after absolution, to begin the repair. The Catechism's list is far wider. It starts with three: Scripture and the Fathers, it says, insist above all on fasting, prayer and almsgiving. They come from the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus says to give, pray and fast in secret, without an audience. One old way to read them: fasting turns you toward yourself, prayer toward God, almsgiving toward your neighbor. Three directions, one turn. Then the list keeps going: making peace, tears of sorrow, concern for a neighbor's salvation, asking the saints to pray, and above all charity. In the Douay-Rheims: "charity covereth a multitude of sins." Then it gets almost ordinary. Conversion happens in daily life, it says: reconciliation, concern for the poor, standing up for what is just, owning your faults, honest correction between friends, looking over your life, examining your conscience, accepting suffering. It quotes Jesus in Luke: "let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." Daily, not once a year. The Church gives the year a rhythm for it: Lent, and each Friday, as days of penance. Reading Scripture counts. The Our Father counts. The Eucharist itself, the Catechism says, feeds this turning. A teenager who apologizes first. A retiree reading the Gospel each morning. Someone who gives up scrolling to sit with a lonely neighbor. All on the list. And the Catechism ends with the prodigal son, who turns toward home and finds his father already running down the road.
screen: `FASTING, PRAYER, ALMSGIVING.` · `CHARITY COVERETH A MULTITUDE OF SINS.` · `IN DAILY LIFE, NOT ONCE A YEAR.` · `LENT AND EVERY FRIDAY.`

segments.voice: Let the list pass slowly: fasting from something small, a prayer, a gift to someone in need, a message that makes peace, an honest look at a fault. Don't pick the most impressive one; notice the one that tugs at you, a little uncomfortable in a useful way, and picture when you could do it. If you pray, offer that small turn to God; if you don't, just keep it in view.
Many forms of penance. Fasting, prayer and almsgiving first, and then a long list of everyday turns: reconciliation, care for the poor, honesty, charity. Today's word.
Your line: many ways back. None of them has to be big. See you tomorrow.

1103.title: Indulgences, honestly (CCC 1471–1479)
1103.hook: not buying forgiveness; a release from lingering effects of sin through the Church's prayer
1103.howItsDone: Catholics may seek an indulgence by doing a prayer or work the Church names, such as a pilgrimage or a work of mercy, together with confession, Communion and prayer for the pope's intentions, and they may offer it for someone who has died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many forms of penance: fasting, prayer, almsgiving, and a long list of everyday turns. Your line was many ways back.

A baseball goes through a neighbor's window. The kid knocks on the door, red in the face, and says sorry. The neighbor says, I forgive you, and means it. The friendship is fine. But the window is still broken, and the glass is still on the floor. Forgiveness happened. Repair hasn't yet. Hold on to that window, because today's word has a reputation, and some of what people have heard about it is wrong.
screen: `A BALL THROUGH THE WINDOW.` → `FORGIVEN.` → `STILL BROKEN GLASS.`

segments.voice: First, what an indulgence is not. It is not forgiveness of sin. The Catechism says it only touches sins whose guilt is already forgiven; the apology and the pardon come first, in confession. So what's left? Catholic teaching says sin has two kinds of consequence. One is the break with God, which forgiveness heals. The other it calls temporal punishment: the leftover damage, the bent habits, the attachments that still pull. The glass on the floor. That needs healing, here or, Catholics believe, in purgatory. An indulgence, the Catechism says, is a release from some or all of it, through the Church: partial, or plenary, which means full. Second, where it comes from. Not from a person's effort alone. The Catechism points to the communion of saints: all God's people, living and dead, bound together, so the holiness of one helps the others. It calls this the Church's treasury: the merits of Christ, and the prayers and good works of Mary and the saints. The Church opens it for a person, attached to a prayer, a pilgrimage or a work of mercy, done with a turned heart. Catholics can also offer an indulgence for someone who has died. Third, the honest part. There were times when indulgences were preached for money, and that abuse became one of the sparks of the Reformation. Martin Luther's protest began there, and Christians still read that history differently. Catholic teaching today is plain: forgiveness was never something a person could buy. An indulgence, done rightly, asks for a changed heart, not a payment.
screen: `NOT FORGIVENESS: THE GUILT IS ALREADY GONE.` · `THE LEFTOVER DAMAGE OF SIN.` · `THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS, A TREASURY.` · `ONCE SOLD. NEVER FOR SALE.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've been forgiven for, by a friend, a parent, a partner, or, if you pray, by God, and then notice what's still on the floor: a habit that keeps pulling, trust still mending, a sharpness you still reach for. Don't scold yourself; just name one piece of glass. If you pray, ask for help with that repair; if you don't, simply notice that being forgiven and being healed can be two different moments.

Indulgence. In Catholic teaching, a release, through the Church's prayer and the communion of saints, from the lingering effects of sins already forgiven. Not forgiveness itself, and not for sale. Today's word.
Your line: never for sale. Forgiven first, repaired after. Go gently, and come back tomorrow.

1104.title: What anointing does (CCC 1520–1523)
1104.hook: strength, peace, courage, union with Christ's suffering
1104.howItsDone: Catholics who are seriously ill, facing major surgery, or weakened by old age can ask a priest for the anointing of the sick, which can take place at home, in a hospital, or during a parish Mass for the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, indulgence, taken honestly: not forgiveness, but healing for what's left after it. Your line was never for sale.

A hospital room, late afternoon, the television muted. The woman in the bed has surgery tomorrow morning. A priest comes in with a small metal case, the size of a lipstick. He prays, lays his hands on her head in silence, then traces oil with his thumb on her forehead and the palms of her hands. Nothing about the surgery changes. So what just happened? Some people think this sacrament is only for the last hour of life. The Catechism tells a wider story.
screen: `A HOSPITAL ROOM.` → `OIL ON THE FOREHEAD AND HANDS.` → `WHAT JUST HAPPENED?`

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred thirty, you met its old name, extreme unction, and learned it isn't only for the dying. Today, what it does. The roots are in the letter of James, in the Douay-Rheims: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." Not a dying man alone: a sick person who calls the community in. The Catechism names the gifts. First, a gift of the Holy Spirit: strength, peace and courage to face serious illness or the frailty of old age. Not a guaranteed cure. Healing of the body can come, it says, if God wills it, but the first gift is inward: the strength not to be swallowed by fear or discouragement. Second, union with Christ's own suffering. Catholic teaching says the sick person, joined to Christ, can find their suffering takes on a new meaning. It isn't wasted. Paul tells the Colossians he rejoices in his sufferings, filling up in his flesh what is lacking in Christ's sufferings, for the sake of the Church. Third, a gift for the Church. The sick person isn't only receiving: joined to Christ's suffering, they contribute to the good of the whole people of God, and the Church prays for them in return. Fourth, for those near the end, a preparation for the last journey, completing the anointings that marked a whole Christian life, from baptism on. So the oil didn't move the surgery. It was meant to change who walks into it.
screen: `IS ANY MAN SICK AMONG YOU?` · `STRENGTH, PEACE AND COURAGE.` · `UNITED TO CHRIST'S SUFFERING.` · `A GIFT FOR THE WHOLE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who is ill, or frail, or waiting on a diagnosis, and picture where they are right now: a bed, a waiting room, a kitchen chair. Think of one plain thing you could say to them that isn't advice. If you pray, ask God to give them strength, peace and courage; if you don't, just hold them in mind.
What anointing does. Strength, peace and courage in illness, union with Christ's suffering, a gift for the whole Church, and for some, a preparation for the last journey. Today's word.
Your line: strength in sickness. The oil is for the frightened, not only the dying. Until tomorrow.

1105.title: Three degrees (CCC 1554–1571)
1105.howItsDone: In the Catholic Church a bishop ordains bishops, priests and deacons by laying hands on them and saying the prayer of consecration; the three serve together in the diocese and the parish.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what anointing does: strength, peace and courage for the sick. Your line was strength in sickness.

Sunday Mass in a parish church. A man in a white alb, a stole worn across one shoulder like a sash, reads the Gospel and later sets the table at the altar. Another, the stole hanging straight down around his neck, says the Eucharistic prayer. And once in a while a third arrives with a tall pointed hat and a shepherd's staff, and it feels like an occasion. Three men, three roles at one altar. A visitor might read three job titles on an org chart. The Church tells it as one sacrament.
screen: `A SASH ACROSS ONE SHOULDER.` → `A STOLE HANGING STRAIGHT.` → `A MITER AND A STAFF.`

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred thirty-one, you met ordination. Today, its shape. The Catechism says Holy Orders is one sacrament in three degrees: bishops, priests and deacons. The bishop's ordination, it says, is the fullness of the sacrament. Catholic teaching sees bishops as successors of the apostles. A bishop teaches, sanctifies and governs a local church, and he alone ordains others. Priests, the Catechism says, are co-workers of the bishops. A priest doesn't minister on his own authority: he works in communion with his bishop, and at ordination promises him respect and obedience. In the parish he celebrates the Eucharist, hears confessions and anoints the sick. Then deacons, and here the Catechism makes a point worth hearing slowly: deacons are ordained not to the priesthood, but to service. In Acts, the apostles ask the community to choose seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to look after the daily distribution of food, so the apostles can give themselves to prayer and the word. Catholic tradition links the deacon's office to that story. A deacon baptizes, proclaims the Gospel, preaches, assists at the altar, witnesses marriages, leads funerals, and gives himself to works of charity. The Latin Church, the Catechism notes, restored the deacon as a permanent ministry, one that can be given to married men. Ignatius of Antioch, whom the Catechism quotes, holds the three together: respect the deacons, the bishop and the presbyters, he says, for without them there is no church. One sacrament, held three ways, for serving one people.
screen: `ONE SACRAMENT, THREE DEGREES.` · `THE BISHOP: THE FULLNESS.` · `THE PRIEST: CO-WORKER WITH THE BISHOP.` · `THE DEACON: ORDAINED TO SERVICE.`

segments.voice: If you know a deacon, picture him: maybe a man who works a weekday job, preaches on Sunday and visits the hospital on Tuesday night. If you don't, picture someone who serves your community without being noticed, who stacks chairs, drives people to appointments, sits with the grieving. 1106.hook: Latin priests are usually celibate; Eastern Catholic churches ordain married men

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred thirty-one, you heard in passing that Eastern Catholic churches have married priests. Here's how that fits. The Catechism tells it as two disciplines, side by side. In the Latin Church, ordained ministers, except permanent deacons, are normally chosen from men of faith who live a celibate life and intend to stay celibate. Celibacy means not marrying, for the sake of the kingdom of God. The Catechism calls it a sign of new life, given over to the Lord and his people with an undivided heart, and points to Jesus's saying in Matthew about those who give up marriage for the kingdom of heaven. Then it turns east. In the Eastern Churches a different discipline has long been in force. Bishops are chosen only from celibates, but married men can be ordained deacons and priests. The Catechism calls this practice legitimate, and says these married priests bear real fruit in their communities. Celibacy is held in great honor in the East as well, and many priests there choose it freely. East and West, a man already ordained can no longer marry. The order matters: marriage first, then ordination. The Gospels hold both pictures. Jesus speaks of giving up marriage for the kingdom. And Peter, the rock, had a mother-in-law: Jesus healed her of a fever in Peter's house. Two disciplines, not two priesthoods, held in one communion. This week ran from the fruits of Communion, through conversion, penance, indulgences, anointing and Holy Orders, to today.
